section.title: The Anointing and the Last Supper
section.sectionRationale: The Passion narrative opens. As the leaders plot and Judas agrees to betray Him, a woman lavishly anoints Jesus for His burial, a beautiful deed set against the ugliness of betrayal. At the Passover, Jesus reinterprets the bread and cup as His body given and His blood of the covenant poured out for many, instituting the Lord's Supper. He then foretells that all will fall away and Peter will deny Him three times.
section.thesis: On the eve of His death Jesus is honoured by a woman's extravagant devotion and betrayed by a friend, and He transforms the Passover into the sign of His own sacrifice, His body given and His covenant blood poured out for many, even as He foretells the failure of all His disciples.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the plot and the anointing at Bethany; Judas's agreement to betray; the preparation of the Passover; the institution of the Lord's Supper; and the prediction that all will fall away and Peter will deny Him.

units.label: The plot and the anointing at Bethany
units.note: a beautiful deed for My burial

verses.text: Now the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread were two days away, and the chief priests and scribes were looking for a covert way to arrest Jesus and kill Him.
“But not during the feast,” they said, “or there may be a riot among the people.”

While Jesus was in Bethany reclining at the table in the home of Simon the Leper, a woman came with an alabaster jar of expensive perfume, made of pure nard. She broke open the jar and poured it on Jesus’ head.
Some of those present, however, expressed their indignation to one another: “Why this waste of perfume?
It could have been sold for over three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor.” And they scolded her.
But Jesus said, “Leave her alone; why are you bothering her? She has done a beautiful deed to Me.
The poor you will always have with you, and you can help them whenever you want. But you will not always have Me.
She has done what she could to anoint My body in advance of My burial.
And truly I tell you, wherever the gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

units.label: Judas agrees to betray
units.note: one of the Twelve went to the chief priests

verses.text: Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests to betray Jesus to them.
They were delighted to hear this, and they promised to give him money. So Judas began to look for an opportunity to betray Jesus.

units.label: Preparing the Passover
units.note: a large upper room, furnished and ready

verses.text: On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, when the {{pascha|Passover}} lamb was to be sacrificed, Jesus’ disciples asked Him, “Where do You want us to prepare for You to eat the Passover?”
So He sent two of His disciples and told them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jug of water will meet you. Follow him,
and whichever house he enters, say to the owner, ‘The Teacher asks: Where is My guest room, where I may eat the Passover with My disciples?’
And he will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready. Make preparations for us there.”
So the disciples left and went into the city, where they found everything as Jesus had described. And they prepared the Passover.

units.label: The Last Supper
units.note: this is My body, this is My blood of the covenant

verses.text: When evening came, Jesus arrived with the Twelve.
And while they were reclining and eating, Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, one of you who is eating with Me will betray Me.”
They began to be grieved and to ask Him one after another, “Surely not I?”
He answered, “It is one of the Twelve, the one who is dipping his hand into the bowl with Me.
The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed! It would be better for him if he had not been born.”
While they were eating, Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, “Take it; this is My {{soma|body}}.”
Then He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, and they all drank from it.
He said to them, “This is My {{haima|blood}} of the {{diatheke|covenant}}, which is poured out for many.
Truly I tell you, I will no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it anew in the kingdom of God.”
And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Then Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’
But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”
Peter declared, “Even if all fall away, I never will.”
“Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.”
But Peter kept insisting, “Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You.” And all the others said the same thing.

pascha.gloss: Passover, from the Aramaic and Hebrew for the feast commemorating Israel's rescue from Egypt, when the blood of the lamb spared the firstborn. Jesus deliberately sets His death at Passover and reinterprets the meal around Himself: He is the true Passover lamb whose blood delivers His people.

soma.gloss: Body. Taking bread, Jesus says, this is My body, giving His disciples a sign of His life offered up for them. The broken bread points to His body given in death, and the Supper becomes the ongoing memorial and means of sharing in that sacrifice.

haima.gloss: Blood. Jesus calls the cup His blood poured out for many, evoking the blood of the Passover lamb and the blood that sealed the covenant at Sinai. His death is a sacrificial, life-giving offering that inaugurates the new covenant promised by the prophets.

diatheke.gloss: Covenant, a binding relationship God establishes. Jesus' blood is the blood of the covenant, echoing Exodus 24 and the new covenant of Jeremiah 31. By His death He seals a new covenant in which sins are forgiven and God's people are bound to Him forever.

basic.context: As Passover approaches, the leaders plot to kill Jesus quietly. At a home in Bethany, a woman pours a jar of costly perfume over Jesus' head. Some scold her for the waste, but Jesus defends her: she has done a beautiful thing, anointing Him beforehand for burial, and her deed will be told wherever the gospel goes. Judas, one of the Twelve, then agrees to betray Jesus for money. Jesus prepares to eat the Passover in a borrowed upper room. At the meal He announces that one of them will betray Him, then takes bread and cup and gives them new meaning: this is My body, this is My blood of the covenant, poured out for many. He institutes the Lord's Supper. On the way out, He foretells that all will fall away and that Peter will deny Him three times before the rooster crows twice.
basic.hermeneutics: Mark frames the anointing between the plot and Judas's betrayal, so the woman's devotion shines against the surrounding treachery. The Last Supper is the interpretive centre: Jesus tells us in advance what His death means, a sacrifice, a Passover, a covenant sealed in blood for the forgiveness of many. The predictions of desertion and denial show that even the closest disciples are sinners He must die to save.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus sets His death at the pascha, the Passover. He gives bread as His soma, body, and the cup as His haima, blood, of the diatheke, covenant, poured out for many.
basic.typology: Jesus is the true Passover lamb, His blood delivering His people as the lamb's blood did in Egypt. His blood of the covenant fulfils the covenant blood at Sinai and the new covenant of Jeremiah. The struck Shepherd fulfils Zechariah's prophecy.
basic.christ: Jesus is the anointed one prepared for burial, the true Passover lamb, and the covenant-maker whose body is given and blood poured out for many. He goes to death knowingly, in fulfilment of Scripture.
basic.god: God's plan of salvation unfolds exactly as written; even the betrayal serves it, without excusing the betrayer. God establishes a new covenant through the blood of His Son, for the forgiveness of many.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 12 gives the Passover lamb. Exodus 24 and Jeremiah 31 give the covenant blood and the new covenant. Zechariah 13 foretells the struck Shepherd.
basic.oneStory: The Passover that rescued Israel from Egypt finds its fulfilment as Jesus, the true Lamb, prepares to give His body and blood for many. In the upper room He seals the new covenant promised long before, in which sins are forgiven forever. The devotion of one woman and the failure of all the disciples frame the meal, showing that the sacrifice He is about to make is for sinners like them, and like us.

context.literary:
Mark builds this section as a sandwich, a device he uses again and again. The leaders' plot in verses 1 and 2 and Judas's offer in verses 10 and 11 enclose the scene at Bethany, so the story of a woman's costly gift is held between two accounts of men planning a death. Each half explains the other. Those who plot want Jesus quietly removed; the woman prepares Him openly for burial. Judas takes money to hand Him over, and she pours out what she has on Him. Mark gives her no name and gives the betrayer his full name and rank, 'Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve,' and the contrast of insider and outsider runs through the whole chapter.

The second half is carried by the repeated phrase 'one of you.' Verse 18 announces a betrayer among those eating, and the disciples ask 'Surely not I?', verse 19, a question that expects the answer no. Jesus answers by narrowing, 'one of the Twelve, the one who is dipping his hand into the bowl,' verse 20, and then moves, in the middle of the meal, from betrayal to blessing, verses 22 to 24. The placement is deliberate: the bread and cup are given while the traitor is still at the table.

The chapter closes with a double prophecy. 'You will all fall away,' verse 27, is softened at once by 'But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee,' verse 28. The disciples' failure is foretold together with their restoration. Peter's insistence in verses 29 to 31 supplies the dramatic irony: the reader knows, because Jesus has said it, that every promise of loyalty will break, and also that the same Jesus will go before them.
context.historical:
Passover was the great pilgrim festival of Israel, remembering the night the LORD passed over the houses marked with the blood of the lamb and brought the people out of Egypt, Exodus 12. The week began with the Passover meal itself, eaten on the evening that began the fifteenth of Nisan, and ran into the seven days of Unleavened Bread. The lambs were slaughtered in the temple in the afternoon, and the meal was eaten in Jerusalem, which is why a room in the city had to be found and why Jerusalem's population swelled with pilgrims. The leaders' fear of 'a riot among the people,' verse 2, is the fear of a city packed with pilgrims who had heard Jesus and who loved Him.

The Bethany meal took place at the home of Simon the Leper, perhaps a man Jesus had healed. The jar of 'pure nard' was a perfume imported from far away, and three hundred denarii was close to a year's wages for a labourer, since a denarius was a day's pay, Matthew 20:2. A woman breaking such a jar and pouring it on a guest's head was doing something extravagant. Anointing the head was the gesture for kings, 1 Samuel 16:13, and for honoured guests, so the deed carried a double meaning, which Jesus himself reads in terms of burial.

The meal in the upper room followed Passover custom. The guests reclined on couches, as free people did on the night of freedom. There were set cups of wine, bitter herbs, the bread, the lamb and a time for recounting the exodus, and the meal ended with the singing of the psalms of praise, which Jews called the Hallel, Psalms 113 to 118. The hymn of verse 26 was very likely part of that tradition. The upper room, found by following a man carrying a water jar, an unusual sight in a world where women normally carried water, suggests an arrangement made in advance, perhaps to keep the place hidden from the plotters.
context.canonical:
The anointing at Bethany is told in all four Gospels with different angles. Matthew follows Mark closely. John names the woman as Mary of Bethany, places the story six days before the Passover and has her anoint Jesus' feet, John 12:3-8. Luke tells a different story of a sinful woman at a Pharisee's house in Luke 7. In every account, the point of Jesus' defence is the same: He is going to die, and she has recognised it.

The Last Supper is told in Matthew 26, Mark 14, Luke 22 and by Paul in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26, which is the earliest written account and shows that the church was already keeping the meal as a received tradition. Paul calls the cup 'the new covenant in My blood,' and John's Gospel gives the teaching of the bread of life, John 6:53-56. In 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 Paul speaks of the cup and bread as participation in the blood and body of Christ and says that one loaf makes the many one body.

Paul names Christ 'our Passover lamb' who 'has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and Peter says believers were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, 'a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:18-19. Hebrews 9:18-22 reads the blood of Sinai as the pattern for Christ's own, and John the Baptist's greeting, 'Look, the Lamb of God,' John 1:29, announces the same. Jesus' promise in verse 25, to drink anew in the kingdom, is matched by Isaiah's feast for all peoples, Isaiah 25:6-8, and by 'the marriage supper of the Lamb,' Revelation 19:9. The prophecy of the struck Shepherd, Zechariah 13:7, belongs to the cluster of texts that Mark's Passion narrative draws on to show that the betrayal and scattering were foretold.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark tells this story to teach his readers how to understand the cross before they reach it. The woman at Bethany sees what the disciples will not: that Jesus is going to die. By giving her act the final word, 'what she has done will also be told in memory of her,' verse 9, Mark makes her the first to respond rightly to the coming passion. She is the model of a disciple who perceives and pours out, while the Twelve debate waste and one of them goes to the priests.

At the supper, Mark lets Jesus interpret His own death before it happens, so that when Mark's readers reach the cross they will not read it as a defeat or an accident. His body is given and His blood is the blood of the covenant, poured out for many. The 'many' reaches beyond the room. Mark's first readers were mostly outsiders to Israel's covenant, and the phrase tells them that the death is for them too.

Mark also wants his readers to take comfort and warning together from the disciples' failure. Every one of the Twelve is told he will fall away, and Peter, the boldest, is told exactly how. The warning is for any believer who thinks his loyalty is secure. The comfort is the promise in verse 28: Jesus will go ahead of them to Galilee. A church made of people who have failed is not a church with no hope, because its Lord goes before it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this chapter describes. The leaders' plot, the woman's deed, Judas's agreement, the preparation, the denial prediction are events and not instructions. The woman's lavish act is praised, but it is not commanded of everyone, and Jesus' remark that 'you will always have the poor with you' is not a reason to neglect them. He says 'you can help them whenever you want,' verse 7, which assumes that care for the poor is ongoing. The line is a defence of one act at one moment, not a policy.

The words at the table are different. Jesus says to the disciples 'Take it,' and later in Luke and Paul He adds 'do this in remembrance of Me,' Luke 22:19 and 1 Corinthians 11:24. The church has understood that to be an instruction for regular practice, and Paul gives instructions on how to keep it rightly, 1 Corinthians 11:27-29. Mark himself records the giving and the drinking, and leaves the command to the other accounts.

Peter's boast and the disciples' sleep are warnings, not models. 'I will never deny You' is the sentence of a person who trusts himself. The proper response is not to resolve to try harder but to see that dependence on Jesus, who is going to go before us, is all there is.

debates.question: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal?

views.label: Yes, on the evening of the Passover
views.case: Mark says so directly: it was 'the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed,' verse 12, and the disciples prepare 'the Passover.' The pattern of reclining, the cup, the bread, the hymn and the setting in Jerusalem fit a Passover meal.

views.label: No, it was a meal the evening before Passover
views.case: John puts the trial before Pilate on the day of Preparation and says the Jews would not enter the Praetorium so as not to be defiled and unable to eat the Passover, John 18:28 and 19:14. On this reading Jesus died as the lambs were being slaughtered, and the Last Supper was a farewell meal with Passover themes.

views.label: Both, using different reckonings
views.case: Some suggest that different groups in Israel counted the days differently, and that Jesus and the Galileans kept the meal a day before the temple authorities. Others say that John's phrase 'eat the Passover' refers to the whole festival meals of the week and not only the first meal.

debates.bearing: Scholars have debated this for a long time and no explanation is without difficulty. What the Gospels agree on matters more: the meal and the death fall in Passover time, and Jesus gives the meal Passover meaning. Whether it was eaten on the Thursday evening or a day earlier, Christ is 'our Passover lamb,' 1 Corinthians 5:7.

debates.question: In what sense is the bread His body and the cup His blood?

views.label: A real presence, by transformation or by union
views.case: The Roman Catholic Church teaches that the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, while keeping their outward appearance. Lutherans teach that Christ's body and blood are truly present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine. Both appeal to 'This is My body,' and to John 6:53-56.

views.label: A memorial and sign
views.case: Zwingli and many later Protestants take 'is' to mean 'signifies,' as in 'I am the vine.' The bread and cup remember His death and proclaim it, 1 Corinthians 11:26. Jesus' own body was standing in front of the disciples as He spoke, which, on this view, shows that the words are figurative.

views.label: A spiritual presence and true feeding
views.case: Calvin and the Reformed tradition hold that Christ is truly present to faith by the Holy Spirit, and believers feed on Him in heaven, not by a change in the elements. Paul calls the cup and bread a 'participation' in the blood and body, 1 Corinthians 10:16.

debates.bearing: All the views agree that the meal is a gift, that it centres on His death for sinners, and that it is received by faith in the company of His people. They differ on how Christ is present, a question the text does not settle. Mark's wording shows what the meal means: the body given, the covenant blood poured out for many.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for the jar in verse 3 is alabastron, a flask of soft stone with a long neck, which was broken open to release the contents, so the jar could not be used again. The perfume is nard pistikes, and the adjective pistikos is an old puzzle. Some think it means 'genuine,' from the sense of trustworthy, and others take it as a technical term for a type or source of nard. The meaning is uncertain, which is why translations say 'pure.' What is clear is the cost.

Jesus calls the woman's act kalon ergon, 'a beautiful deed,' verse 6. Kalos means fair, noble, and fitting, and not merely useful, which is the register of her critics' calculations. They say 'waste,' apoleia, a word also used for ruin and destruction. Jesus' reply shows a different measure: love does not count in waste. In verse 8 He says she 'came beforehand' to anoint, prolambano, the verb 'to take in advance,' and the noun entaphiasmos, 'preparation for burial.' The woman's anointing of a living man is read as the burial anointing that no one else will have time to do, since when the women come with spices on Easter morning, Mark 16:1, the tomb is already empty. The word 'Christ' itself means the Anointed One, so the deed has a layered irony, the anointing of the Anointed.

At the table the verb in verse 22 is eulogeo, 'bless,' for the bread, and in verse 23 eucharisteo, 'give thanks,' for the cup, which is where the church's word eucharist comes from. In verse 24 the blood 'is poured out' is ekchynnomenon, a present participle, so that He speaks of the pouring as already happening, as if the future were present. The preposition is hyper, 'on behalf of,' with 'many,' polloi. The phrase echoes Isaiah 53:11-12, where the Servant justifies 'many' and pours out His life unto death. Mark 10:45 says the Son of Man gives His life as a ransom for many.

'Blood of the covenant' is the wording of Moses at Sinai, Exodus 24:8, which the Greek Old Testament closely matches, and the Hebrew word for covenant, berith, is rendered by diatheke, which means more than a contract: a settled arrangement set by one party. Mark does not say 'new,' as Luke and Paul do, but the Jeremiah promise of a new covenant, Jeremiah 31:31-34, which includes the forgiveness of sins, stands in the background, and Matthew adds 'for the forgiveness of sins,' Matthew 26:28.

In verse 27 'fall away' is skandalizo, from skandalon, a snare or stumbling block. The disciples will be tripped up by what happens to Jesus. Peter, in verse 31, 'kept insisting,' in the imperfect tense of repeated action, so the claim is repeated and not said once.

typology.fulfillment: The Israelites chose an unblemished lamb, kept it until the fourteenth day, killed it at twilight, and put its blood on the doorframes, and the destroyer passed over those houses, Exodus 12:5-13. The meal was kept every year as a memorial. Jesus takes the same night and the same meal and sets Himself at the centre. Paul says, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and Peter says believers were redeemed by the blood of 'a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19. The escalation is that the deliverance is no longer from Pharaoh but from sin and death. The type falls short in that the lamb's blood protected a household for a night, while the blood of Christ secures forgiveness for many and for good.

typology.type: The blood of the covenant at Sinai, Exodus 24:6-8
typology.fulfillment: Moses took the blood of the sacrifices, sprinkled half on the altar and half on the people, and said, 'This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you.' Jesus uses almost the same words over the cup. Hebrews reads Sinai as a pattern: even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood, Hebrews 9:18-22. The correspondence deepens in Christ because the covenant's blood is now His own, and what Sinai sealed with promises to obey, which the people broke, He seals with the forgiveness of sins. The type falls short because the blood of animals could not take away sin, Hebrews 10:4.

typology.type: The struck Shepherd and the scattered sheep, Zechariah 13:7
typology.fulfillment: The prophet speaks of a shepherd, 'My Companion,' struck by the sword at the LORD's command, and of sheep scattered. Jesus applies the verse to the night ahead: the disciples will scatter when He is seized. The correspondence is almost word for word. The escalation in Christ is that the striking is part of God's saving purpose and not only a disaster that befalls a leader. And the promise 'I will go ahead of you into Galilee' recasts the scattered flock as a flock regathered by their shepherd. The type reaches beyond the flock of that night, since the Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11.

typology.type: The banquet of the kingdom, Isaiah 25:6-8
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah foresaw a feast on the LORD's mountain for all peoples, at which He will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears. Jesus' vow in verse 25 not to drink the fruit of the vine until the day He drinks it new in the kingdom turns the Last Supper into a promise of that banquet. The supper looks back to the exodus and forward to the feast. The fulfilment is seen in Revelation 19:9, the marriage supper of the Lamb. The type is still unfolding, since the great feast is not yet held.

typology.type: The anointed king and the anointing for burial, 1 Samuel 16:13
typology.fulfillment: Samuel poured oil on David's head and the Spirit rushed upon him, marking him as God's chosen king. At Bethany an unnamed woman pours perfume on Jesus' head, and Jesus reads it as a burial rite. The same act that in Israel marked a king is here the mark of a Messiah whose throne is the cross. The correspondence is a sign that His kingship and His death are not opposed. The type has its limit: David's anointing led to a throne in Jerusalem, while Jesus' anointing led to a tomb, and only after it to the throne at God's right hand.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first as the one who knows where He is going. At Bethany He explains the woman's act as preparation for His burial, and at the supper He says the Son of Man 'will go just as it is written about Him,' verse 21. He is not carried by events. He announces the betrayal, arranges the room, names the cup, and tells Peter what the night will hold. The cross is not an accident of history; it is His own chosen way, as He said in Mark 10:45, 'to give His life as a ransom for many.'

It leads to Christ as the Passover lamb. The meal that recalled the exodus is turned into a meal that proclaims His death, and the apostles read it just so. John's Gospel shows Jesus condemned on the day of Preparation, when the lambs were slaughtered, John 19:14, and Paul and Peter call Him the lamb. The story of Israel's rescue from slavery becomes the pattern of a greater rescue, and every detail of the meal, the bread broken, the cup shared, now speaks of Him.

It leads to Christ as the maker of the covenant. The blood poured out 'for many' is the blood that seals a promise, and Jeremiah named the promise: a law written on hearts, God known by all, and sins remembered no more, Jeremiah 31:33-34. Hebrews says He is 'the mediator of a new covenant,' Hebrews 9:15. Jesus does not simply teach about forgiveness; He pours out His life to make it possible.

It leads to Christ as the Shepherd who goes before. Even while He foretells their failure, He promises to lead them into Galilee. The risen Lord keeps that promise in Mark 16:7, and the message to the women singles out Peter by name, 'tell His disciples and Peter.' The one who was denied is the one who goes ahead to meet the deniers.

It leads to Christ as the Anointed. The woman anoints Him, and the title Christ means anointed. She does what the leaders and the disciples will not: she recognises that the Messiah must die. A caution applies. The jar is not a coded symbol, the upper room is not an allegory, and the details of the meal are not secret references to Christ. The passage points to Him by His own words, by the way the Passover and Sinai are quoted, and by the New Testament's reading of the supper. And the intimacy is plain: He gives His body and blood to those who will leave Him within hours, and drinks nothing more until He can drink it with them in the kingdom.
study.god:
This passage shows a God whose plan holds firm through human treachery. The betrayal is not a surprise that overturns the plan, since the Son of Man goes 'just as it is written about Him,' verse 21. Yet the betrayer is not excused: 'woe to that man.' The text holds the two truths together without resolving the mystery of how. Acts later says that Jesus was 'delivered up by God's set purpose and foreknowledge' and that men acted lawlessly in putting Him to death, Acts 2:23. God's sovereignty does not turn Judas into a puppet, and Judas's guilt does not make God's plan fragile.

It shows a God who keeps covenant. The blood of the covenant at Sinai had bound Israel to obey, and Israel had broken it, Jeremiah 31:32. God does not abandon His people for that failure. He makes a covenant in which He Himself provides what He asks, putting His law within them and forgiving their sins, Jeremiah 31:33-34. The cup in the upper room is the God of Exodus and Jeremiah keeping His word.

It shows a God who provides the sacrifice. In Israel's own story God had once provided a ram in place of a son, Genesis 22:13, and had provided a lamb for each household in Egypt. Now He provides the lamb who is His own Son. This is the heart of the gospel as Paul states it: God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The supper is not a story of men appeasing an angry God but of God giving.

It shows a God who knows His people's weakness and loves them. Jesus knows that all will flee and that Peter will deny Him, and He gives them the bread and cup nonetheless. His promise to go ahead of them to Galilee is made in the full knowledge of their failure. God's faithfulness is not a reward for disciples who hold on; it is the ground on which failing disciples can be held.

It shows a God who values the costly gift. Jesus does not call the woman's perfume a waste, but 'a beautiful deed.' God receives what is poured out in love, and He has His own measure of worth, which differs from a ledger of efficiency. The same God who commands care for the poor also receives extravagant worship, and the two are not rivals.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to approach the table with both gratitude and honesty. We come as those who may betray and deny, and we are welcomed by the One who gives His body and blood anyway. The meal looks back to His death and forward to the feast: we proclaim His death until He comes, 1 Corinthians 11:26.

crossReferences.note: The Passover instructions: an unblemished lamb, killed at twilight, its blood on the doorframes, and a feast kept as a lasting memorial. Jesus eats this meal on the night He is betrayed and puts Himself in the place of the lamb, so that the memorial of Egypt becomes the memorial of the cross.

Moses sprinkles the blood on the people and says, 'This is the blood of the covenant.' Jesus' words over the cup, 'This is My blood of the covenant,' are nearly the same. He claims for His own blood the role that the sacrificial blood played at Sinai, but at far greater cost.

The promise of a new covenant, with the law written on hearts and sins remembered no more. Luke and Paul call the cup the new covenant, and the forgiveness Matthew adds to this saying, Matthew 26:28, is the promise of the last line of Jeremiah's passage.

The Servant justifies many, bears their iniquities and is poured out unto death. Jesus' 'poured out for many' echoes both the word 'many' and the language of pouring out in these verses. It is one of the strongest links between the supper and the Suffering Servant.

The prophecy Jesus quotes in verse 27: strike the Shepherd and the sheep will be scattered. By citing it, Jesus tells the disciples that their flight is not a surprise to God, and that it fits the pattern of Scripture.

The psalmist's close friend, one who shared his bread, has lifted his heel against him. John applies it directly to Judas, John 13:18. In Mark's account, 'the one who is dipping his hand into the bowl with Me' recalls it, so that the betrayal is shown as the Psalm's experience come true.

God prepares a banquet for all peoples and swallows up death forever. Jesus' promise to drink the fruit of the vine anew in the kingdom, verse 25, looks to this feast. The table in the upper room is a promise of the table that has no end.

Paul's account of the supper, written before any Gospel, shows the church already keeping the meal. He adds the command to remember and the statement that each time we eat and drink we proclaim the Lord's death until He comes, tying the meal to both past and future.

'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.' Paul uses the Passover and its unleavened bread as a pattern for a holy life. The line shows that the early church already understood the supper as the true Passover.

The writer reads Sinai as proof that a covenant needs blood, and ends with the principle that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. The passage explains why Jesus' words over the cup speak of blood, and why the death was necessary.

John tells the anointing with the woman named as Mary, the feet anointed and Judas as the one who objects, with the added comment on his motives. The parallel confirms Jesus' own interpretation of the act as preparation for burial.

The angel's word to the women, 'tell His disciples and Peter, He is going ahead of you into Galilee.' It is the fulfilment of Mark 14:28 and shows that the failure foretold in this chapter does not have the last word.

'Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.' The unfinished meal of Mark 14:25 reaches its end here, where the Lamb and His people sit together at the feast Jesus promised to drink anew.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story began with a man and woman at a table in a garden, where eating the wrong food broke fellowship with God. Genesis 3 is a meal gone wrong. The story of redemption is the long work of bringing a people back to a table. The Passover was the first great step: a meal eaten in haste on the night of rescue, with the blood of a lamb on the door. Sinai added a second meal, the covenant meal on the mountain, where Israel's elders 'saw God, and they ate and drank,' Exodus 24:11. Jesus' last meal gathers these threads.

The chapter answers the question that the sacrificial system had left open. Year after year the lambs were killed and the blood was shed, and Hebrews says that the blood of bulls and goats could not take away sins, Hebrews 10:4. The old covenant pointed forward to a better blood. At the table Jesus says that the blood is now His own, the covenant is now sealed, and the many for whom it is poured out include those who will abandon Him in a few hours. This is the story's turning: the covenant that Israel broke is remade by God Himself at the cost of His Son.

It also sets up what follows. The Gethsemane scene, the trial and the cross are the events the supper has already interpreted, and the resurrection the Shepherd promises, 'after I have risen,' is mentioned in the same breath as the scattering. The church that comes from this night will meet around the same bread and cup, carrying the memory of the death and the hope of His return.

The new creation is a banquet. Isaiah saw a feast on the LORD's mountain where death is swallowed up forever. Jesus said He would not drink again until He drank it new in the kingdom, and John sees the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. In the final city, God dwells with His people and wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:3-4. The scene of betrayal, denial and abandonment in the upper room is not the end of the table but the cost of it. Those who eat the bread and drink the cup in faith are being fed, at the price of His body and blood, for the day when the table is full and no one is missing.

quiz.q: How did Jesus interpret the woman's anointing at Bethany?

options.text: As a beautiful deed anointing His body in advance for burial, to be told wherever the gospel is preached.
options.note: Mark 14:8-9; Jesus honours her devotion and ties it to His coming death.

options.text: As a kind gesture that was, however, somewhat wasteful.
options.note: Others called it waste; Jesus called it beautiful and meaningful, rebuking their criticism.

options.text: As an act of love that pointed to His burial.
options.note: True, but it should include Jesus' promise that her deed would be told wherever the gospel goes.

options.text: As a distraction from caring for the poor.
options.note: Jesus defended her against exactly that charge, affirming her act toward Him.

quiz.q: What did Jesus say the bread and the cup represented at the Last Supper?

options.text: His body given and His blood of the covenant poured out for many.
options.note: Mark 14:22-24; the Supper signifies His sacrificial death sealing a new covenant.

options.text: A memorial of the exodus from Egypt only.
options.note: He transformed the Passover to point to His own body and blood, not merely the past exodus.

options.text: His sacrifice that inaugurates a new covenant of forgiveness.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should name specifically His body given and His blood poured out for many.

options.text: Ordinary food with no special significance.
options.note: Jesus gave the bread and cup profound meaning as His body and covenant blood.

quiz.q: What is the significance of Jesus setting His death at Passover?

options.text: He is the true Passover lamb whose blood delivers His people, as the lamb's blood spared Israel in Egypt.
options.note: The timing and words identify Jesus as the fulfilment of the Passover, 1 Corinthians 5:7.

options.text: It was simply the season when He happened to be in Jerusalem.
options.note: Jesus deliberately tied His death to Passover to reveal its meaning.

options.text: It connects His death to the feast of Israel's redemption.
options.note: True, but it should name Jesus specifically as the true Passover lamb whose blood delivers.

options.text: It shows He wanted to reform the Passover ritual.
options.note: He fulfilled and reinterpreted the Passover around Himself, not merely reformed a ritual.

quiz.q: How does the anointing relate to Judas's betrayal in Mark's account?

options.text: Mark frames the woman's costly devotion between the plot and the betrayal, contrasting love with treachery.
options.note: The sandwich structure sets her beautiful deed against the surrounding scheming.

options.text: They are unrelated events told one after another.
options.note: Mark deliberately intertwines them to contrast devotion and betrayal.

options.text: Both show different responses people had to Jesus.
options.note: True, but it should note the deliberate contrast of extravagant love against betrayal.

options.text: Both show that following Jesus is about money.
options.note: The contrast concerns devotion versus greed, not that discipleship is about money.

quiz.q: What did Jesus foretell about His disciples that night?

options.text: That all would fall away and Peter would deny Him three times before the rooster crowed twice.
options.note: Mark 14:27-30; He foretold both the general desertion and Peter's specific denial.

options.text: That Peter would deny Him three times that night.
options.note: True, but it omits that all the disciples would fall away, fulfilling Zechariah's struck Shepherd.

options.text: That one disciple would betray Him but the rest stay faithful.
options.note: Jesus said all would fall away, not only that one would betray Him.

options.text: That the disciples would boldly defend Him to the end.
options.note: The opposite; He foretold they would all desert Him.

questions: The woman gave something extravagantly costly to Jesus, and others called it waste. What would wholehearted, even lavish, devotion to Christ look like for you?
Judas was one of the Twelve, close to Jesus, yet betrayed Him. How does his example warn you against nearness to Jesus without a true heart?
Jesus gave His body and blood for many, including disciples who would fail Him. How does it move you that He died knowing you too would sometimes fail Him?
Every time the church shares the bread and cup, it proclaims the Lord's death. How can you come to the Lord's Supper with deeper understanding and gratitude?
Peter was confident he would never fall, yet he did. Where might overconfidence in your own faithfulness be leaving you unguarded?

translationNotes.note: My blood of the covenant echoes Exodus 24:8; some manuscripts read the new covenant, making explicit the fulfilment of Jeremiah 31:31. Poured out for many recalls the servant of Isaiah 53 who bears the sin of many.
The betrayer is identified as one of the Twelve who dips in the bowl. The shared bowl heightens the horror of betrayal by a table companion.

I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered quotes Zechariah 13:7; the scattering of the disciples fulfils prophecy, and Jesus at once promises to gather them again in Galilee after He rises.
